P1.evidence: No setter notes or application referenced at any point; the only pre-call material mentioned was raised by the prospect himself ('the videos that from that you guys have me watch before this meeting'). The frame ran two parts plus the disqualification promise — 'go into what you would like to achieve, where you're currently at. See if we can help you bridge that gap... If I feel like we're just not the right fit, I'll point you in the right direction, okay?' Agreement taken and the open question asked. Worth crediting separately: he asked how to pronounce the prospect's name before starting, which is not on the checklist and set the tone well.

P2.evidence: Age, height and weight all asked directly. Injuries pursued with a proper sweep — 'do you have current back aches, pains, anything come up besides the back as well?' then 'do you have other places that you feel aches and pains?' — which surfaced the neck and the knees. Training history and diet both handled well, including the treat question. The cardiovascular 1-10 scale was a good improvisation and produced a 2 out of 10 plus the three-flights-of-stairs admission. The failures are serious for this prospect: work was never asked about, so the 80-hour week and the sedentary radiology role arrived only because he volunteered them; health conditions were never asked of a man carrying roughly 80 lb of gained weight; and sleep was never asked despite the prospect raising it twice unprompted, including naming it as a goal.

P3.evidence: The bridge was the best-delivered version of it in the batch, close to the script's own wording: 'a lot of people that we speak to, of course, the physical is always a byproduct of a bigger why for someone. So do you think you have a bigger why for yourself?' It produced the ten-year account, the college clothes he has kept and 'I'm only 32 years old. So I should be in my peak physical.' The impact question was asked leadingly — 'want to be a good role model, et cetera, for when you do potentially get some' — and the prospect corrected him into something better: 'if you want to be a dad and your kid wants to go kick football and you can't even do it because you're out of breath.' The one clear miss is the reflect-back. The college clothes were the emotional centre of the call and were never given back to him as the point.

P4.evidence: What he had actually tried across ten years was never enumerated — 'I've tried' passed without follow-up. Why it did not stick was pursued properly though: 'do you think it would have been impossible for you to have, like, 40, 45 minutes of just working out regularly, even during that time period?' produced the 80-hour weeks and the two-hour commute, and the prospect named the constraint himself. He also volunteered that the constraint has now lifted — ten minutes from work, gym in the building — which is the single most useful fact in the call and the rep did pick it up. The information line never ran.

P5.evidence: The consequence question ran and was well set up: 'let's say you don't make the drastic changes that you also know that you do need to make... where do you think that you would be at in like six months to a year from now?' returned 'More back pain, worse sleep, probably even more weight, to be honest. Probably just overall unhappy as well.' The settle question followed, though phrased confusingly enough that the answer 'I think so, yeah' is ambiguous about which clause he was agreeing to. No why-not, no line in the sand.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran cleanly before the price — 'outside of that, do you feel like, yes, Richard, this is something I see myself doing and I actually see myself getting the results of fitting into old clothes, getting confidence?' — answered 'I think I can. I can put in the work and do my part.' The 1-10 gate returned 8.5 with an honest caveat about never having tried the modality, which the rep probed and resolved with scale evidence before moving on. He had a clear yes and only then went to the number, which is exactly the sequence the script asks for.

P11.evidence: The offer was refused outright, so no payment or onboarding step was reachable.

objection_plays.detail: The isolation ran twice and ran well, including the hypothetical form — 'let's say, out of the blue, six grand would fall on your lap, would you be like, okay, Richard, let's just go?' — which correctly separated want from capacity and got a yes. The open-conversation ask ran near verbatim: 'if you want to, we can at least have a conversation about it. See if, because this is not the only thing we do, maybe there's something else we could fit in there.' And he asked the budget question, which produced a real number: 'a couple hundred dollars. The high end, maybe it's like sub a thousand.' What did not run: the SHOULD-I versus HOW reframe, the break-it-up line, and every one of the six financial-picture questions — no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no card count, no available credit, no investments. Instead of mapping what he had, the rep went straight to two forms of borrowing. Credit to him for stopping cleanly when both were refused rather than pressing.

Price transparency. The prospect's final substantive point was that nothing anywhere told him the price before he committed an hour: 'if I had known the cost, I would have never, ever set the meeting up, taken somebody's spot.' There is no play for this and there is nothing a closer can say to it, because it is a funnel design decision rather than an objection. It belongs to whoever owns the marketing. It is also directly traceable: the sales manager said on 22 June that the publicly visible price is $200 a month and that 'it doesn't really matter if somebody comes in thinking it's a certain price', and this prospect arrived expecting a couple of hundred dollars.

notes: Process-wise this is one of the better calls in the batch — Phase 3 and Phase 6 both ran close to complete, the bridge question was textbook, and he had a genuine 8.5 out of 10 before naming the price. It was lost on qualification, not on execution: a resident doctor working 80 hours a week who expected to pay a couple of hundred dollars was never going to be a $6,000 buyer, and nothing in Baseline or in the setter handover surfaced that before an hour had been spent. The two coachable items are small by comparison. Ask about work, and reflect back the college clothes he has kept for ten years rather than summarising the goal list.
